items.stem: Define the term 'capacity utilisation'.
items.answer: The proportion of maximum possible output that is actually being produced: current output ÷ maximum output × 100.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition – The proportion of maximum possible output that is actually being produced: current output ÷ maximum output × 100. 1 mark: partial definition or a relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain why high capacity utilisation can reduce unit costs.
items.answer: Fixed costs such as rent and machinery are spread over more units of output, so the fixed cost per unit, and therefore average cost, falls.
items.markingKey: 1 mark fixed costs spread; 1 mark lower average cost. [2]

items.stem: Explain one problem of operating at 100% capacity utilisation.
items.answer: There is no time for maintenance and no spare capacity for extra orders, so machines may break down, staff may be stressed and new orders may be turned away.
items.markingKey: 1 mark problem; 1 mark explanation. [2]

items.stem: Rising costs of imported packaging have cut its profit margins. Lagos Bites Ltd, a private limited company in Nigeria with about 700 employees, produces packaged snacks such as plantain chips and chin chin. Explain the effect on the costs of Lagos Bites of an increase in capacity utilisation.
items.answer: Points to develop for Lagos Bites: capacity utilisation = output ÷ maximum output × 100; fixed costs spread over more units; lower average costs allow lower prices or higher margins; at very high levels costs may rise from overtime and breakdowns.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: capacity utilisation = output ÷ maximum output × 100. AO2 Application [1]: point linked to Lagos Bites (food processing). AO3 Analysis [1]: developed explanation of the consequence, e.g. fixed costs spread over more units; lower average costs allow lower prices or higher margins. [3]

items.stem: Define the term 'excess capacity'.
items.answer: When a business's current output is below its maximum capacity, so some resources are under-used.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition – When a business's current output is below its maximum capacity, so some resources are under-used. 1 mark: partial definition or a relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain two ways a business could respond to excess capacity.
items.answer: It could increase demand through promotion, price cuts or new markets so more output is sold; or reduce capacity by rationalisation, such as closing a factory.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark response, 1 mark explanation): increase demand, rent out space, make products for other firms, rationalise. [4]

items.stem: Explain why a business might not want to increase its capacity even though demand is greater than capacity.
items.answer: The extra demand may be temporary, so new capacity would later be under-used; and building capacity is expensive and risky.
items.markingKey: 1 mark temporary demand; 1 mark cost/risk. [2]

items.answer: Points to develop for Hamid Engineering: a capacity shortage means demand exceeds capacity; overtime or extra shifts in the short term; subcontracting or outsourcing; investing in new capacity in the long term.

items.stem: Define the term 'outsourcing'.
items.answer: Using another business (a third party) to carry out activities that were previously done within the business.
